MR. PROBE-REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON MARCH 2
speechtext:
I rise to a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. Yesterday the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson), while I was temporarily absent from this chamber, made a charge, as reported at page 1786 of Hansard that I had, in effect, called the management and shareholders of H. R. MacMillan Export Company gangsters. I quote from the relevant portion of the hon. member's speech:
This man MacMillan and his so-called gang paid $7,660,000 in taxes to the federal treasury and yeit the hon. member for Regina Oity calls them a bunch of gangsters.
On the next page the hon. member is quoted as saying:
I think that if anyone is referred to as a member of a gang, he is a gangster.
In my speech on February 5 last, this is what I said, as reported at page 926 of Hansard:
In other words, the profits of the MacMillan gang who clipped the coupons were within fifty cents per share of the men who wenit out bo the fields and the forests and the mills to do the w'ork . . .
And so on. I realize, Mr. Speaker, that there is a natural tendency to give to words a meaning not always necessarily in accord with the intent of the speaker or writer, but rather in accord with the limited education, the type of experience and the nature of the past association of the listener. That is doubtless true of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni.

maintopic: MR. PROBE-REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON MARCH 2
speechtext: Order. The hon. member has stated his question of privilege, and he should not make any statement.

maintopic: MR. PROBE-REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON MARCH 2
speechtext: I think it is necessary to give a definition of this-

maintopic: MR. PROBE-REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON MARCH 2
speechtext: Order. The hon. member has stated his question of privilege and should be satisfied.

maintopic: MR. PROBE-REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON MARCH 2
speechtext:
My point of privilege has not been stated, Mr. Speaker. It is this. I
did not, according to any standard dictionary which contains the word "gang" or otherwise, use that word in a sense that would give the imputation of gangster referred to by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, nor had I any such intention. Therefore I ask through you, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member withdraw the imputation which he made with regard to myself.

maintopic: MR. PROBE-REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON MARCH 2
speechtext: When I went to school, Mr. Speaker, I always understood that the singular of "gang" was "gangster". I am afraid I have not had access to the vast education of my hon. friend.

maintopic: MR. PROBE-REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON MARCH 2
speechtext: That is obvious.

maintopic: MR. PROBE-REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON MARCH 2
speechtext: However, if he feels so badly about the matter, I should be glad to withdraw if he will also withdraw the imputation he made that the shareholders of the MacMillan company were members of a gang.

maintopic: MR. PROBE-REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON MARCH 2
speechtext: I made no imputation whatever, Mr. Speaker, that the shareholders of the MacMillan company were members of a gang.

maintopic: MR. PROBE-REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON MARCH 2
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: MR. PROBE-REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON MARCH 2
speechtext: I am happy that the hon. member has apologized.

maintopic: MR. PROBE-REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON MARCH 2
speechtext: I would call attention of hon. members to a rule which says that when the Speaker rises, the member who has the floor should resume his seat. It is important that this rule should be observed so that we may have order in this house. The hon. member has stated his question of privilege and should be satisfied. Now he is asking that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni withdraw certain remarks. It is not the practice to ask, on the day following, for the withdrawal of what has been said during debate on the day before.

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): Mr. Speaker, I would like to communicate to the house two letters I received just a short while ago from the former minister of Czechoslovakia, addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The first, bearing date of March 3, 1948, is as follows:
Your Excellency,
I have the honour to inform you that I am announcing today to the Czechoslovak government in Prague my resignation, as envoy extraordinary and minister plenipotentiary of Czechoslovakia in Canada.
At the same time, Dr. Vladimir Moudry, first secretary, ;andi Dr. Karel Bala, commercial attache, are announcing their resignation to their respective departments of the Czechoslovak government in Prague.
The legation will be in charge of Colonel Jiaromir Petzold, MBE, who remains at his post.
I would appreciate it very much if you could kindly inform His Excellency the Governor General about my resignation, and convey to him my grateful thanks for all his kindness, which he has extended to me on so many occasions.
May I express to Your Excellency my warmest thanks for all your co-operation and assistance in my work in this country.
Accept, Excellency, the renewed assurance of my highest consideration.
Frantisek Nemee.
The second letter bears the same date and is also addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs:
Your Excellency,
Referring to my letter of March 3, I have the honour to announce to you that from the staff of the legation Miss Alzbeta Katzova and Miss Eva Blumenscheinova, both office secretaries at the legation, are sending their resignation today to their respective departments of the Czechoslovak government in Prague.
Frantisek Nemec.

speechtext:
1.	What is the name of the steel controller for Canada?

subtopic: STEEL CONTROL
speechtext:
1.	Frederick Kingston Ashbaugh.
2.	There is no steel control board.
3.	None (See answer immediately preceding).
4.	Steel slabs are being diverted from Sault Ste. Marie to Hamilton enabling steel producers there to increase their production of plate and other steel products.
Ingots and billets from Sydney are 'being diverted to Hamilton and Montreal for conversion into finished steel.
The use of a Bessemer converter at Sault Ste. Marie is speeding the open-hearth cycle there and will result in increasing ingot production up to a level of 70,000 gross tons per month.
Subsidization of scrap has resulted in the movement of a considerable tonnage into Canada as well as stepping up the flow into steel-making areas from outlying districts.
An additional blast furnace is being repaired and additional coke ovens installed at Sydney and will go into operation in the near future. Efforts are being made to arrange the adding of primary steel facilities at Hamilton.

subtopic: LIFE INSURANCE-LOANS TO POLICYHOLDERS
LIFE INSURANCE-LOANS TO POLICYHOLDERS
speechtext:
1. What rate of interest are life insurance companies allowed to charge on loans to policy holders whose premiums are paid (a) by contract, if the rate of interest is named for loans in the text of the policy; (b) if loan is made not according to text of contract?

2. What was this rate during the last war and after the last war, and what is the increase, if any, in such rates charged policy holders for loans?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: LIFE INSURANCE-LOANS TO POLICYHOLDERS
speechtext:
1.	(a) If the rate is specified in the contract, the company may charge any rate not exceeding the specified rate but in practice no life insurance company, whether Canadian, British or foreign, transacting business in Canada charges Canadian policyholders a rate in excess of 6 per cent effective per annum and a great many companies charge only 5 per cent even where a higher rate is specified.
(b)	All policies of life insurance issued by companies, except some issued many years ago, contain a provision for policy loans and the maximum rate of interest is invariably specified. In cases where there is no loan provision and hence no specified rate, the practice is the same as described in (a), namely, to charge a rate not exceeding 6 per cent effective per annum and in many companies the rate is only 5 per cent.
2.	Prior to January 1, 1936, the rate of interest on policy loans varied up to 8 per cent per

Questions
annum but in 1935 all life insurance companies transacting business in Canada gave an undertaking to the government that the maximum rate would be reduced as from January 1, 1936 to 6 per cent effective per annum, such reduction to apply to both outstanding and new loans. The great majority of companies charged rates varying from 5J per cent to 6 per cent during the early years of the war of 1939-1945 but in 1944 many companies reduced the rate further to 5 per cent. There has been no important change since then, either by way of increase or decrease.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, last night when the debate adjourned I was trying to repair some of the damage which had been done by the Tory member for Queens in an address which he had made a day or so previously regarding conditions in the province of Prince Edward Island.

I had shown that 9,373 cars of potatoes were shipped across the straits last crop season, a larger number than had been shipped in any previous year. Incidentally, the potato crop of Prince Edward Island last year amounted' to about 10,000,000 bushels.
The Tory member for Queens had attempted to belittle the federal government, but in doing so he belittled his own province. I was reminded of the oration of John Bright in the British House of Commons when he was depicting the condition of the Irish people a few generations ago at the hands of the British government. As far as the. federal government's dealings with Prince Edward Island are concerned, I shall speak of my own constituency.
Since I came into the house in 1935 the federal government has constructed seven boat harbours in my constituency for the benefit of the fishermen, and I do not think my hon. friend can point to one boat harbour on the whole island which his party has ever constructed. I have just received notice that a new boat harbour will be constructed at Launching Place, the contract having been awarded to H. J. Phillips and Son, the lowest tenderer, at 863,853.30, so that both the county

and the province as a whole will benefit from this new harbour. There is another boat harbour in my constituency being constructed at Bayfield at the present time. It is being done by day labour, the men are now getting out the lumber and the money has already been voted.
I think the Liberal party rather than the Conservative party should claim the title "progressive", but the Liberal party does not believe in changing its name. It is only bank robbers and bandits and people with too many letters in their names who want to change them. On the contrary, the Conservative party on several occasions, have made their name longer. For example, in 1920 they changed their name to the National Liberal and Progressive Conservative party of Canada. The Liberal party brought in old age pensions, family allowances and many other social benefits, and that is why I say they should claim the title "progressive".
Speaking of socialism, I listened yesterday for a short time to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I am not finding fault with his speech because I admire him. However, he seems to be opposed to free enterprise. I cannot understand why the C.C.F. party should be opposed to free enterprise because I do not think there would be one of them here today if when he was born his veins had not been full of free enterprise. There was one thing the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre admitted! unwillingly, that is, that the Liberal party would be in power until 1971.
The Tory member for Queens (Mr. McLure) stated that he did not have time to deal with the question of mail couriers and fishermen. If there is any party in this house who should keep away from the mail courier question, it is the Tory party. We all remember the last session before the 1930 election. They brought in an amendment to the Post Office Act to place the mail couriers in the civil service,, but like all opposition amendments it was voted down. In the early part of the campaign every mail courier in Canada had in his possession a letter signed by the leader of the Conservative party giving the details of that resolution and saying that if they came to power they would put them all in the civil service. I tell you, sir, it was dangerous to meet a mail courier on the road during that campaign.
But what happened1? Shortly after the Tories came into power the mail couriers began to ask to be placed in the civil service, but instead of placing them in the civil

The Address-Mr. Grant
service they threw out all their contracts to tender to keep them quiet. I know that many of these poor men could not get any money. I know one man who was getting 31,100 and who heard that his neighbour was going to tender for $500, so he tendered for $480 and got the contract. But today under a Liberal government that same man is getting $1,400 under the new regulations brought in last year by the Post Office Department.
My hon. friend-

speechtext: The Tory member for Queens.

Yes, the Tory member for Queens. He wants to have a share of the glory of those new regulations. When he sees that we are trying to do something he decides to get in on it and take some credit. He claims credit for the 9,393 reefer cars that were brought to the island last year.
The affairs of our fishermen are something else that they should keep away from. During their term in office between 1930 and 1935 the fishermen of Canada were starving and they did not do one thing for them. They let them starve. Their boats were rotting at the wharves when we got into power in 1935. When we came into power we instituted the fishermen's loan board and we helped the fishermen to build new boats, and when the war came along they were just beginning to be prosperous again. My hon. friend would try to persuade the fishermen that his party would do a lot for them. We are trying to get the Department of Fisheries to buy canned fish in the maritimes and send it overseas for relief purposes. If that is done, then my hon. friend will want to take the credit.
I see the Tory member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) is in his seat. If there is one man in this house who does not like the word "Tory" it is my hon. friend. You cannot mention the word "Tory" without his hair standing on end. I am reminded of the farmer who was working in his fields when a young man came along and put his hand on his shoulder and asked him what he was doing. The farmer said, "I am doing my work." The man said, "I am a farm inspector; stop your work and show me around." He showed the farmer a card which read, "So and so, farm inspector." The farmer looked at the card and said, "I guess that is enough," and he went with him. They looked at all' the fields and finally came to a pasture field where there were a lot of cattle. The inspector man jumped over the fence to go to look at the cattle standing in the shade of a canopy which the farmer had erected. When he got near the cattle a 5849-1174
male animal came toward him. It was advancing pretty fast and the inspector thought he should retreat.

The advice given me by one of my old teachers is that when you heard nothing, you should say nothing. However, it is hard to resist when the hon. member across the way, who I understand is an authority on nails, drives one in.
In some countries there is a bird known as the vulture. It is a stout bird and it watches around for some other bird of its own size to build a nest and lay its eggs and then it goes in and eats the other bird's eggs and lays its own eggs and then loafs around until the other bird hatches out the young ones and rears them. I was just thinking that perhaps those are the tactics that have been adopted by the Tory member for Queens. He waits around until he finds that something is going to be done and then he slips into his seat and asks the minister a question about it for the benefit of his constituents.
I notice my time is getting short, and I want to say something to the government. This government is not perfect any more than any other human organization. I want to say a word about the sale of canned fish. There is going to be difficulty in selling all this fish in this country. The canneries are about to start up operations and an appeal is being made to the Department of Fisheries to buy our surplus canned fish to be sent overseas for relief purposes. I hope the government will take note of that, as it is of vital importance to our canners and fishermen.
For some years we have had a car ferry by means of which a very good trade has been worked up between eastern Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia. But it is only a summer boat and in the fall she ceases to operate. We have however two winter ports, Georgetown and Pictou, in the near vicinity, and our people want the government to put
The Address-Mr. McCullough

on this route in winter, one of the winter boats which is idle at Borden. A largely signed petition has been presented to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) asking for this service, and the board of trade has also asked for it, and I trust that the minister will accede to that request.
There are other matters with which the government should deal. One is the sales tax, that Tory sales tax. It should be abolished, and I hope it will be abolished this year. Everyone who goes out to spend a dollar finds himself short by at least eight cents because of that tax. Then there is a luxury tax of twenty-five per cent on refrigerators and other household furnishings. These taxes should be taken off to give the people a chance to live. Prices are so high at the present time that the government has started an investigation into the cause and a committee is now looking into that matter. Why not at the same time reduce or abolish some of these taxes that perhaps we can get along without?
As I have said, this government, being a human organization, is not perfect.
The ancient philosophers' conception of the perfect man was in the possession of those powers and qualities which are required for the honourable discharge of his duties in life, each in the golden mean, equally removed from excesses and all in due proportion. If any hon. gentleman in this house can be placed in that category I think it is our Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie Eng), who may not be with us at the next session of parliament. He has devoted almost fifty years of his life to the welfare of humanity. He has been a wise peacetime leader, and second to none as a wartime leader. In this regard his name is a household word in every civilized country in the world. He has not sought titles, but he has won for himself the only title that has any lasting value, the title of "Good and faithful servant".

Mr. Speaker, the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne permits members to bring before the House of Commons any grievances which they may have. I have very many grievances; and may I say that we have come out of the war in a privileged position and that if we take pains and do the necessary planning we can as it were become a torch to the free peoples of the world. It is because of that I rise today not as a Canadian representing only my own constituency but hoping rather to speak what is in the minds and what are the desires of the great majority of the Canadian people.
It is true that the present Liberal government has many problems, problems which are complex not only as they relate to Canada but also as they relate to the international picture. Since 1939 we have seen the light of freedom go out in many countries throughout the world, and that has been very distressing to us, but here in Canada we have been fortunate in escaping the tragedies which have overtaken many countries in Europe and Asia. Therefore I want to bring to the attention of the government some of the things I feel should be done to allow the people of Canada to share in a post-war prosperity which, as I say, will be a light to a darkened world.
I want to refer to the veteran, the old age pensioner, the worker and the farmer.
In the first place I feel that the veteran has not been allowed to have that share in the post-war reconstruction of this country to which he is entitled and which Canada could easily afford. We have seen in Canada sledgehammer blows, one after another, struck at our Canadian economy. Principally because of the decontrol measures of this government the veteran has been put in an almost hopeless position, where he is not able to buy a house or house furnishings, or rehabilitate himself on a farm and buy the necessary farm machinery. We have seen costs continually going up so that his gratuity and re-establishment credit have not been sufficient to enable him to rehabilitate himself.
Old age pensioners too have been shamefully treated) by this government. While the government saw fit to introduce a bill increasing the pension by $5 a month, already that increase has been eaten up by higher costs of living.

The Address-Mr. McCullough
It is the same with our workers. During the war the workers across this country were willing to accept the freezing of wages, just as the farmer was willing to accept the freezing of prices in order to win the war, but both the farmer and the worker expected fair treatment in the post-war period, and they have not got it.
I was at a demonstration at an airport the other day where it was indicated that one of the large aeroplanes called the North Star would cost approximately half a million dollars to build in Canada. So here we see the same thing happening now that happened during the war-all kinds of money to build these things, but when it comes to rehabilitating hundreds of people who went and fought for freedom, not very much is done.
I had a return brought down the other day in answer to these questions:
1.	How many applications have been made each year, by provinces, for the Veterans Business and Professional Loans Act?
2.	How many of these applications have been granted, by provinces, to date?
I find in my own province of Saskatchewan that the number accepted is 269, and the amount of the loans given to these veterans is $461,218, a mere pittance; less than half a million dollars to rehabilitate all the veterans who have applied under this Veterans Business and Professional Loans Act to rehabilitate themselves. The act is not working, sir. I have had veterans come to me asking whether they could get a loan to rehabilitate themselves. The return I received indicates the sort of niggardly assistance that is being given under the provisions of this act.
The workers of this country by and large accepted the freezing of wages-[DOT]

This afternoon I intend to speak particularly of the farming or agricultural conditions in this country because I feel that the great mass of workers and farmers are interdependent. Since agriculture is the backbone of the country the prosperity of the worker is certainly dependent on the farmer. Therefore it is certain that we must have prosperity in agriculture in order for the worker to have a decent standard of living. As a fanner I say the workers and the people of this country are our best customers. We want them to receive decent wages so that they can buy the beef, butter, pork, cheese and other farm commodities which we produce.

I want to give a brief resume of what has taken place in the field of agriculture. In western Canada we came through deplorable years during the depression when we had my hon. friends to the right in power, and later the Liberal party which is now in power. During those tragic years the farmers of western Canada were taking absolutely ridiculous prices to feed not only the people of Canada but also of the world. I shall not give all the figures, but I do want to give some. These figures are actually what the farmer got for his various commodities. I think, Mr. Speaker, it would be well to put these on the record as a whole, if I can get the unanimous consent of the house, because all the figures that have been given, so far as I am aware, have been for wheat and coarse grains f.o.b. Winnipeg, Port Arthur and Vancouver. The figures I am about to quote give the net returns to the farmer. I wish to refer to some of them.
Shortly after the Tory party came into power the farmer was getting 47 cents a bushel for No. 1 northern wheat. In 1932 he got 38 cents; in 1933-34, 47 cents, and so on. In 1930 the farmer got 15 cents a bushel for oats; 18 cents in 1931, 13 cents in 1932 and 19 cents in 1933. For barley he received 12 cents in 1930, 21 cents in 1931 and 19 cents in 1932. The other day the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) asked me what the farmers were getting for rye at the present time, perhaps indicating that the open market and the grain exchange were giving a market for the farmers' rye. I wish to tell the house here and now that I myself have marketed rye for 12 and 15 cents a bushel on the open market. I think I speak for the majority of western farmers when I say that we never want to see a return of prices which are contained in the table which I shall put on Hansard. Here are the prices that obtained on the open market: in 1930, 17 cents; 1931, 23 cents; 1932, 24 cents. That is the sort of thing we have had from the Winnipeg grain exchange. Is it any wonder that not one of us from western Canada, who has worked to produce these things, wants to see the Winnipeg grain exchange remain open? We want to see the Winnipeg grain exchange closed. Today we are getting S5 for our flaxseed. I understand we are going to get another 50 cents. I believe the government would be well advised to consider this suggestion that, in the event of the costs of production rising for the next few years, as they will do largely because of the government's failure to maintain the ceilings, any difference there may be between what the farmer receives for his wheat and the increased cost of production should be made up out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.
That was our position then; that is our position today. I cannot see how the government or any member on the other side of the house can feel that the farmer is being fairly dealt with when this decontrol is allowed to go on and the farmer's prices are going up with the result that today we have agriculture precipitated into utter chaos. We have assistance given to big businesses in this country to the extent that we have double depreciation; with regard to the excess profits tax, today we are asking the people of this country to pay back the twenty per cent which is refundable. As indicated in the 1947 Canada Year Book, under the chapter on assistance to private investments:
Special depreciation allowances for tax purposes were granted between November, 1944, and March 31, 1947, for projects completed prior to March 31, 1949. Over this period of approximately two and one-half years, approvals for special depreciation had reached a total in excess of $1.300,000,000. Low- interest rates and special credit facilities for industrial expansion, not provided by the commercial banks, were made available through the establishment of the government-sponsored industrial development bank, a subsidiary of the Bank of Canada, in 1944.
I think if we can do these things for big business, it is time we did something similar for agriculture in this country. Today we find that agriculture cannot get cheap credit. On account of the higher cost of farm machinery farmers are finding that replacement is coming so high that they are again being loaded with a terrific debt in western Canada. I have here some figures which indicate what is taking place. These were provided to me through Canadian Co-operative Implements Limited of Regina. As an example, we find that the price of an AR 2-3 plow John Deere tractor after the 12) per cent increase in 1946, which I feel was completely unjustified, again *when the ceiling came off went up from $1,480 to $1,750, or an increase of S270. I have here a survey which was made by the dominion government, or at least was put out by the dominion Department of Agriculture, which indicated the number of tractors which would be needed in various provinces. In my own province for the years 1947 and 1948, the pent-up demand for combines I find to be 18,508. The difference in price of a Massey-Harris self-propelled combine as between 1947 and 1948 amounts to $415.50. This one item in western Canada, if that pent-up demand for combines is supplied, would amount to approximately $7,708,574. So we should look into conditions of living on the farms in western Canada.
I have here figures taken from the United Farmers of Canada information bulletin on Saskatchewan agriculture. I find that in 1945 the net farm income from the sale of farm products per average farm amounted to $2,155, the average of his net from 1940 to 1945 being $1,338. That is for one and a half adult males on a farm. Breaking that down we find that for every male adult on the farm the net income was $892. Surely if these figures are anywhere nearly correct, and even allowing
The Address-Mr. McCullough

for disparities and differences with regard to the authenticity of the figures, we can still see that the farmers in western Canada are in a poor condition having regard to income. In view of the record of production of western Canada, I think we are not getting a square deal. I find here, in compiling the estimates, that the farmers of Canada during that same period from 1940 to 1946 inclusive, shipped for export 64,000,000 head of livestock. That number, marching in single file, would reach twice around the world1. So it was a magnificent effort on the part of our people. During the same period the farmers produced for export 4,300,000.000 pounds of meat products. This quantity would1 equal a train one half mile long arriving at seaboard every week day for seven years. In regard to wheat exports during that same period of 1940 to 1946 inclusive, we shipped for export 1,477,175,280 bushels.

As I have indicated, profits in big business have been allowed to run wild, while at the same time the farmer is still getting the small end of the stick. The other evening I was much interested when the hon. member for Resti-gouche-Madawaska (Mr. Michaud) rose in his place and showed great concern about the fertilizer situation in his province. On several occasions in this house I have protested the action of the government in selling the three fertilizer plants built in this country during the war. Not once did any other

The Address-Mr. Fulton
hon. member, either on the government side or in the official opposition, seem concerned about the price of fertilizer. On every occasion I indicated that I felt sure a monopoly was being built up in Canada by the sale of these plants. I expressed the concern of the Canadian federation of agriculture as shown in letters to the Minister of Agriculture and the then minister of munitions and supply with respect to the sale of these plants. I should like here to quote a few words from the speech of the hon. member for Resti-gouche-Madawaska, at page 703 of Hansard for January 29, 1948, referring to ammonium nitrate:
The biggest price jump wias in connection with this latter ingredient, where the increase was a Little more than fifty per cent. On this point I wish to read from the tetter of Mr. Walsh who, in referring to ammonium nitrate, said:
"This represents the most violent price advance and in the farmer's eye the least justified. The three Canadian plants were built by Britain to supply nitrate during the war if her own plants were bombed."
Then he goes on to say:
"Farmers do not believe that the $91 price is justified." That is the present price; it jumped from $69 to $91.
All I can say to the hon. member and those who up to now have not been concerned about this matter is that this indicates the trend of government policy in this country. They sold down the river the people's own plants which were built with the taxpayers' money during the thirties, in order to allow them to get into the hands of monopoly interests in this country. So far as I am concerned there is only one thing for the government to do. My information is that already, in two years of operation, the Welland plant has made enough to pay back the cost of the plant together with 825,000 which was spent on reconstruction. If the government wants to protect the people of this country they should take back that plant immediately and reimburse the company as they may see fit. I am concerned about the situation with respect to fertilizer in this country. Unless we can keep the price at a level which will permit the farmers to use it we are going to continue to deplete our soil. The hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska referred to potash. In my own province of Saskatchewan we have immense beds of potash, another essential ingredient going into the fertilizer mix. If the federal government would make an appropriation similar to some of the appropriations made for the necessities of *war we could develop those beds and not only conserve United States dollars but also conserve our own soil.
I want to conclude by saying this. Recently the new farm income tax forms have been sent out. I have some of them here; I tried to get from the minister's office every type that has gone out to Canadian, farmers. Looking through them all I find that only the farmer, so far as I am aware, has to fill out an income tax return which in my opinion is not only discriminatory but also insulting. I know a good many farmers; I am one myself, and I think the average farmer is a fair person. He does not like to pay taxes any more than any other person, perhaps, but on the whole he will do what is fair. But when we ask the farmers as a class to fill out this farmer's net worth statement, I think it is insulting. It says, under current assets, "Cash on person or on farm". I do not think it is fair or even reasonable to expect farmers to fill out any such income tax form. If the farmer fills out am income tax form such as that of last year, showing gross income and gross assets, and then his expenditures and net income, he is giving the government all the information they should have, and if he does not fill that out he can be prosecuted under the present act. This is a miserable sort of thing.
If we want to find out where the money is in this country, I think there is one policy we can follow. The government can call in the money of all denominations over five dollars. It can say that three months hence every person having money in denominations over five dollars shall come and exchange it in our banks for new currency, and then we shall find out where the money is. That, I say in conclusion, is what the action of the government should be if they do not feel that the farmer is being just.

It is now nearly three months since the address in reply to the speech from the throne was first moved in this house, and the aspect which I wish to discuss this afternoon for a few minutes is not the address itself but the amendment to it that we are debating, because that amendment is, in effect, a vote of want of confidence in the government. It is, therefore, important to go over the speech from the throne, which we are now considering, and find out why it is that we of the official opposition consider that the program there set forth, coupled with the government's past record, is not such as to command the confidence of the house.
When one analyses the speech from the throne he finds that it is aim jst a completely negative quantity in so far as suggesting constructive steps for the future development of Canada is concerned. I read it over care-
The Address-Mr. Fulton

fully only yesterday, and again today, before speaking, and I was able to find in it only two paragraphs which contain the outline of a program of a positive nature.
I should like to go over it paragraph by paragraph, to have a look at it, in order to see how much we can find in it that will be helpful to the future of Canada, where there is an indication of any positive program to build up the country, any indication that we have faith in the future of Canada as a great country, as having a future which we can bring about, not by accident, not merely by letting events take care of themselves, but by a positive series of steps taken in our lifetime, the results of which we shall be able to see.
Looking over the speech from the throne with that in mind, what do we find? In the first paragraph it refers to conditions throughout the world. They "continue to be difficult and disturbing". That is informative but not very constructive. We are told that Canada was recently represented at a meeting in Australia to discuss peace with Japan. There is another paragraph with regard to the united nations, and the fourth paragraph tells us of the unsettled conditions that still prevail in Europe and Asia; again a fact which, while informative, is not very constructive.
The next paragraph contains the first suggestion of a constructive nature. That paragraph refers to the Geneva trade agreements and is. I think, one example of a positive forward-looking step. Whether or not one agrees with it entirely, it certainly can be said to be an effort looking toward the expansion of our trade, and therefore something that will contribute in a positive sense to the building up of Canada.
Then we have a reference to the exchange conservation measure, and next to the shortage of United States dollars. The next paragraph tells us that the government has progressively removed controls made necessary by the war and has done so in a "gradual and orderly manner", which not only is not very constructive, but is even highly controversial.
Then we have a reference to the United Kingdom food agreements. The only other reference to a constructive proposal in the speech from the throne is the next paragraph, which says that we shall be asked to consider plans for a low-rental housing project for veterans.
Then we have a reference to the so-called national labour code, which, while very important, is a matter which will only adjust an existing situation. It will not contribute to positive material development in the future of a constructive nature.

Then we have a reference to demobilization, which was concluded in September, and some references to agriculture and fisheries legislation, dealing partly with efforts to bring about more orderly marketing and so on, but no reference to the positive building up of those industries.
So we have only two references to any constructive program. There is nothing which indicates that the government has confidence that by a program which it initiates it can contribute to the building up of this country, and that it intends to do so. It is largely for that reason; it is for what we do not find in the speech from the throne, that we feel that the program of the government and the government itself do not command the confidence of the house or the country.
There are specific reasons which can be put forward in support of a motion of want of confidence. One of the first is the sorry condition of the veterans. There is certainly no one in the country who has less cause to have confidence in the government than the veterans of both great wars. The setting up of the veterans affairs committee will give us an opportunity for a general discussion of veterans affairs, and the bill before the house providing for limited increase in pensions will afford an opportunity to discuss that particular matter. Therefore at this moment I am not going to go into any detail with respect to that subject, but before I leave it I want to say that the latest increases, in fact the total increases in pensions announced are to most of us, if not to all of us, a matter of very grave disappointment; and I think that for the veterans themselves they constitute a very serious, a very real cause of frustration.
I am not surprised that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), in announcing the last series of increases in pensions, carefully refrained from giving the house the figures at the time he was reading his statement. It will be remembered that the first time, before Christmas, he gave the figures as well as the statement; but after Christmas there was simply a statement read and the figures were tabled, appearing in Hansard the next day, so that there was no immediate opportunity to debate or comment on those figures. It is not surprising, I say, that he did not give out the figures and so give us an opportunity to question him and to point out that there was nothing but a little bait dangled before the veterans, affording the government an opportunity to say, "We are giving you some increases"; for when it is analysed you will find that, while it is true that the pension is increased by a dollar or two dollars a month, it is no

The Address-Mr. Fulton
real assistance to the veterans in solving the problem of meeting the increased cost of living.
From that point of view the speech from the throne, and the program we have since seen so far as veterans are concerned give us cause for nothing but lack of confidence in this government. Casting around for a simile or a description which one might apply to the speech from the throne and the lack of program which it revealed, one is left without adequate words. It has all the interest; it has all the enthusiasm; it has all the rousing qualities of last week's washing, and it is just about as limp. It reveals the government as being without a policy.
Another great lack in the speech from the throne is its complete ignoring of all questions of foreign affairs, its failure to reveal Canadian foreign policy. In view of what is happening in Europe today I think that lack should be immediately remedied. There should be without delay a statement from the minister outlining Canada's foreign policy with particular reference to current events in Europe.
We have seen events taking place step by step which are almost an exact parallel-I do not wish to use words which are incautious or unwise, but I think these are accurate-an exact parallel of what took place from 1935 to 1939. So far, Canada appears to have accepted the steps which have been taken. Other countries have issued strong statements which leave the world in no doubt as to what their policy is, in no doubt as to whether or not they accept the steps which have been taken, but as yet no such statement has been issued on the part of this country.
This afternoon the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) read a letter from the ambassador of Czechoslovakia to Canada announcing his resignation. That can surely be taken as a protest on the part of that gentleman against the events which have recently taken place in his country. That proper and courageous gesture cannot but have the admiration of all Canadians. I think all Canadians would be only too happy to see a similar courageous and proper move on the part of Canada in the way of a statement on foreign policy and on that particular matter.
In addition to what has taken place in Europe, there are other events which have taken place in South and Central America, in the Falkland islands and British Honduras. We cannot afford to ignore developments in the world today. We are frequently told that middle and lesser countries look to Canada 5849-118J
for guidance and leadership. Whether they do or not, and I think it is probably true that they do, it seems to me that Canada must take a position with respect to what is going on. Canada cannot expect to have a position in world affairs unless she takes a stand and makes that stand known.
In passing, I should like to say that I wish to echo what was said last night by the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Case), that it is a great pity that we withdrew our occupation troops from Europe and thus lost that windowpane through which we might keep an eye on events in central Europe. By doing that we lost the opportunity of having a number of Canadians over there who could see for themselves what was going on in Europe, which would have been a tremendous help to our people in assessing and understanding what is actually taking place and in evaluating and working out a policy which might help to deal with events over there.
We remember what happened in the years before 1939 when step by step events occurred which led inevitably to war. It has been said by many qualified to know, that one of the contributing factors to the war was the uncertainty on the part of nations generally as to what would be the attitude of other nations, particularly the nations of the British commonwealth, and the middle powers. It seems to me that those events prove the necessity of having a statement now on foreign policy while we still have an opportunity to make it. I repeat my request that such a statement be made without delay.
I have indicated some of the reasons why I feel the speech from the throne contains in it nothing of any force and, therefore, why I support the motion of want of confidence which has been moved. However, in addition I should like to outline two steps of a constructive nature which I think should be taken and which would assist in building up this country in a positive way. One is the construction of a trans-Canada highway, and the other is the extension to the rest of Canada, particularly to British Columbia, of the provisions of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.
I have a resolution on the order paper advocating the construction of the trans-Canada highway and therefore I will not devote a great deal of time to that subject this afternoon, but the history of past sessions has showm that it is doubtful whether we shall have an opportunity of discussing private members' resolutions, and since I have waited for two years for an opportunity to discuss
The Address-Mr. Fulton

this matter, I should like to say just a word about it now.

I thank you, sir, for your guidance. I shall not refer to the resolution itself, but I think I am at liberty to discuss the general situation. I first brought this matter u.p in 1946 in an effort to discuss it while the estimates of the Department of Transport were being considered. My suggestion at that time was that we should have a trans-Canada highway policy and: that the administration of that policy should be under the Minister of Transport. That is why I sought to discuss it at that time, but it was ruled that such a discussion would be out of order because there was no item in the estimates of that department which had to do with highways. Accordingly, at the beginning of the 1947 session I placed a resolution on the order paper advocating that the dominion government should develop a trans-Canada highway policy and should immediately enter into negotiations with the provinces for the construction and maintenance of trans-Canada roads. It will be remembered that at that last session it was announced that, owing to the pressure of government business, no opportunity could be given for the discussion of private members' resolutions. Therefore I renewed my resolution and it stands in the same form on the order paper of this session.
There is across this country a great and growing body of opinion which supports the idea that there should be a trans-Canada highway system and that the dominion government should make a contribution to the construction of that road or roads. This is of particular interest to my constituency and to all of British Columbia, because highway construction there is more difficult and, therefore, more expensive than in most other provinces. I should1 like to read one resolution I have received, because I think it outlines the situation very neatly and suggests a proper solution. It is a resolution from the Central North Thompson board of trade, at Clearwater Station, British Columbia, and has been sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen), as well as to the Premier of British Columbia, myself and the provincial member for Kamloops. It reads as follows:
This board of trade wishes to draw your attention to the many requests from all parts of Canada, looking to the completion of a tr-ans-

Canada highway, and urges upon the governments of both the dominion of Canada and the province of British Columbia, to bake steps to further the formation of a highway commission that would have the power to carry to completion the construction of a trans-Canada highway, which is such an urgent necessity to our country.
And we urge that such a commission should adequately survey the various routes available, and at once bring up to standard, the route judged besit to serve the people of Canada with an all-Canadian highway.
We believe, sir, that only by co-operative action between the dominion and provincial governments can a highway be built adequate to the needs of the country, and we ask your earnest consideration of these apparent needs.
The letter is signed by the secretary of the Central North Thompson board of trade. I know that many members have received similar resolutions, and since the matter is of particular importance to my province and that part of the country in which I live, I have had many similar resolutions-from the Revelstoke board of trade, the Salmon Arm board of trade, the Blue River board of trade and the Kamloops board of trade, to mention only a few-along the same general lines. One should not overlook, in discussing this matter, the work done by the Calgary board of trade, which I believe was the first board to start a dominion-wide campaign some two or three years ago for a trans-Canada highway.
The position is complicated by what I might call a certain amount of competition as between various routes which have been suggested. I should like to mention and at the same time to pay tribute to those who are now advocating what is known as the Yellow-head route for the trans-Canada highway. They have sent to members of parliament a pamphlet outlining the advantages of that route and supporting, in general outline, federal aid in the construction of a trans-Canada highway. At this point I should like to read a resolution on this subject contained in the policy declarations of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. I am reading from the policy declarations of the seventeenth annual meeting held at Winnipeg in 1946. I believe that a similar resolution is contained in the policy declarations of 1947, which I have not now at hand. But in 1946 the Canadian Chamber of Commerce passed the following resolution, headed, "A National Highway Program":
Be it resolved that the Canadian Chamber of Commerce recommends that the dominion government immediately negotiate with the provincial governments on a mutually acceptable basis for the development of a national, transcontinental highway construction and maintenance program.

The Address-Mr. Fulton
And be it further resolved that such a na-tionial transcontinental highway program provide for the maintenance and extension of the Alaska highway.
I read that particular resolution because, like the one from the Clearwater board of trade, it puts the matter in its proper light and avoids conflict between various groups. What it is concerned with is to obtain acceptance of the general principle that there should be a federal trans-Canada highway program and that a scheme of federal aid should be worked out with the provinces on a mutual basis for the construction and maintenance of such a road. Once that principle is accepted, it will be a matter for the dominion and provincial experts to decide what route or routes should be adopted; but, until we have accepted the general principle, I suggest that to enter into such details would only delay the issue and perhaps involve us in a discussion of matters we are not qualified to determine. It may well be found, once the principle is accepted and a survey is made, that there should be more than one route. I am going to suggest in a moment that there are good reasons why there should be more than one trans-Canada highway, but I think the discussion should be confined at the moment to the acceptance of the principle of federal aid in the construction and maintenance of trans-Canada roads.
It is interesting to observe that the Canadian House of Commons in 1912 and again in 1913 gave its approval by a recorded vote to the principle of federal aid in the construction of a trans-Canada road. The government of Sir Robert Borden in 1912, through the then minister of transport, introduced a bill to provide for future aid to the provinces in the construction of a main trans-Canada road. The bill passed the house, all parties accepting the principle on the second reading without a division, but the bill was defeated in the Senate. The then minister of transport reintroduced the bill in 1913 and it met exactly the same fate, being defeated again in the Senate. It will be remembered that at that time the government of Sir Robert Borden had been in office for only a year or two and that in the other chamber there was a majority of a political persuasion opposite to that of the government, which may or may not have had something to do with the defeat of the bill. At least these two facts went side by side; and the bill passpd the house but was defeated in the Senate. The important point to remember is that the House of Commons in two successive sessions accepted the principle of federal aid to the provinces in highway construction, and if the principle was
acceptable and such aid was felt to be necessary then, surely it is equally acceptable but far more necessary now, when highways are much more important to the maintenance of our economy than they were before.
Another precedent which might be urged in support of the idea is the practice in the United States, where the federal government makes a 50 per cent contribution to the state governments for the construction and maintenance of federal highways.
Some of the concrete reasons why there should be such a national transcontinental road and a dominion highway policy are, first, for purposes of defence. After all, if there is a next war, should a next war come, if it takes the form often ascribed to it of heavy aerial attacks our railways will be vulnerable, and it seems to me that we should have an alternative trans-Canada route, a first-class highway or possibly two or more as our population warrants. Second, it would be an additional encouragement to tourist traffic. Third, because of the important contribution made to our economy and to the maintenance of our trade and commerce by the trucking industry. An adequate first-class trans-Canada route is required for that purpose. Fourth, to enable our population to move more freely about the country. In this connection I wish to make this point, that if the federal government would assist in the construction of main trans-Canada roads the provinces would be able to bring the secondary roads, the north and south roads, up to adequate standards, which in turn would assist in the development of the back country much more rapidly by enabling our population to move in and develop it. Canada's history has been that of population following the lines of communication. The railways have made a tremendous contribution to our development. I think it is fair to say that without them we would not have had the development we have in Canada today. But you cannot build a railway to every nook and cranny in Canada.
If the federal government would assume a portion of the responsibility of constructing and maintaining main roads the provinces could go ahead with their proper share of responsibility, which is the development of the back areas, enabling the country to be opened up and a great constructive development to take place.
I should like to refer again to the particular position of British Columbia which, as I said, is mountainous and sparsely populated. We find it very difficult and expensive per head of present population per mile of highway construction. And it can easily be seen that federal assistance in such a matter would be of tremendous benefit to our province.

The other matter of a constructive nature that I wanted to mention this afternoon is the extension to the rest of Canada, and particularly again, from our point of view, to British Columbia, of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. In passing, I should like to observe I realize it may be charged, as it has been in the past, that members of the opposition, myself included, are constantly criticizing the government for extravagance, saying you should economize, and then coming forward with suggestions which will involve further expenditures. The point I make in reference	to	that is	that we do	advocateeconomy. We advocate economy where there is improper extravagance. It is easy enough to mention some of the cases: government publicity, overcrowding of the civil service, unnecessary appointments where they exist, and so on. We have never advocated the curtailment	of	proper	development	of	ourresources	by	what would amount	to	falseeconomy. We advocate proper expenditure, compensated	for by	proper economy.	It
certainly could not be charged that these expenditures are inflationary, because, unlike normal government expenditures, these would be productive, and I have never heard it said that anything which contributes to the wealth of the country in a real sense is inflationary.
In speaking thus, and asking the government to extend to British Columbia the provisions of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, I should like to renew the plea that I made approximately a year ago in the house along the same lines. Speaking here on March 6, 1947, I outlined the principles which I felt could be usefully followed in extending the act to British Columbia. The first of these principles was that it should be viewed as a long-term project and financed possibly by issuing bonds which are redeemable in series over a period of years, perhaps up to fifty years, so that you do not saddle the land or the country in one year or in a few years with the cost of this development.
Second, it should be regarded as an integrated project; that is, any construction done under the P.F.R.A. should be worked into an integrated project along the lines of the projects in the United States, which have to do with both irrigation and the development of power. Here again, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say this. Some people say that we are advocating tremendous expenditures before the population of the country warrants it. May I point out that surely the history of Canada shows that where we have been bold and courageous and built railways and made capital expenditures in advance of population, population has rapidly followed

and taken advantage of the resources which have been provided for it. I want to say this: to my mind all these matters involve and are made feasible only by a courageous appreciation of the necessity of Canada having a larger population, and the taking of steps to provide it.
I said that we criticized the speech from the throne because we feel it does not contain anything constructive. We believe that Canada can be built into a great country in our own time, and these are some of the steps which we should like to see taken to bring about that result. We are not building just for ourselves. We suggest that w-e build for a great nation in the future as well, for our children and our children's children, and to make it possible also for more people to come to this country, to make it possible for us to absorb them and provide them with the opportunities for useful production.
In the same way that population formerly followed rails, they will now' follow roads, but to an even greater extent I think they will follow power. Industry will follow power. In British Columbia we have a tremendous power potential as well as lands available for irrigation, so that our province particularly is lying there waiting for something like an integrated project which may be brought about under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.
The history of the matter, in so far as extension of the act to British Columbia is concerned, is a little disappointing. In 1946 it w'as indicated that legislation would be introduced 'at the next session, that is, in 1947, to extend the act to British Columbia. In 1947 w'e kept pressing the minister. He indicated that he hoped to be able to bring down proper legislation. On May 22, however, he made a statement which definitely precluded that possibility. On May 22 the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said that the dominion government would be will-to enter into negotiation or consultation with the provinces on individual projects which they might bring forward, but that there would be no general legislation extending the act to British Columbia. Why that should be I am unable to understand. I obtained the most recent report of the administration of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1947. On page 1 of the report I find an outline of the principles of development as laid dow'n by the administration of the act. It reads as follows:
Water development-A program designed to effect the conservation of the limited -water resources of the prairies for farm domestic stock-watering and irrigation purposes. Ad>-

The Address-Mr. Fulton
visory engineering and financial assistance for prairie farmers and rural communities in the construction of (logouts, dams and irrigation works.
It seems to me that these principles are as fully applicable to interior British Columbia as they are to the prairie projects.
When dealing with the expenditures so far made under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, one finds that to date in Manitoba there has been spent $135,134.36; in Saskatchewan, $3,893,815.94; in Alberta, $786,890.98, or a total of $4,815,841.68 in the prairie provinces. In the same period there has been spent in British Columbia $58,298.04. That has been spent on a project at Pemberton Meadows, where the engineers of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act are assisting the local community in reclaiming land where it has been flooded, and enabling it to be brought under cultivation again. For that assistance the people of the interior, and I think it would be correct to say the people of the whole province, are grateful, but we still hope for and we still ask for the extension of the principles and the enabling legislation of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act to the province as a whole.
There are other local schemes in which the prairie farm rehabilitation administration are assisting, in conjunction with the Department of Veterans Affairs, in putting small local irrigation projects into operation to enable land to be irrigated which has been taken up under the Veterans Land Act. There are two such projects in the immediate vicinity of Kamloops, and I think two others in the Okanagan valley, but these are very small projects in comparison with the total area available for irrigation.
It is estimated that in the interior of British Columbia there are nearly 100,000 acres available for irrigation in the Thompson and Okanagan valleys alone; in the vicinity of Salmon Arm, Kamloops, Ashcroft, at Lillooet on the Fraser river and at points in the Okanagan. These lands are now available; they are waiting for irrigation. They have also other resources which, if power could be brought in at the same time, would enable the agricultural population and the agricultural industries to be complemented and balanced by the development of light secondary manufacturing industries. After all, we do not want to see, and I do not think the house or the country as a whole wants to see, our emphasis laid exclusively on further development of the agricultural population. It seems to me that what we want is a balanced economy so that, whereas at the moment we are
almost entirely dependent on export markets for our produce, we could, if we had greater industrial development out west, support a greater industrial population. Thus we could consume at home more of the food we produce, and at the same time use on our farms more machinery produced at home; or to put it the other way, produce at home more mechanical equipment for use in agriculture, as well as food, clothing, et cetera, for our increased population. In this way we would be a little less vulnerable to world depressions. I am not suggesting that we should isolate ourselves or close ourselves off, but I suggest that at the moment we are perhaps the most vulnerable nation in the world to a worldwide depression. If we would balance our economy a little bit better, we would be a little less vulnerable.
Our province, together with so many other areas throughout the west, is literally crying for irrigation and power development, which would enable us to put our agriculture on a stable, sure foundation and at the same time to build up the secondary industries and balance off the increased agricultural production. So I hope that the Minister of Agriculture this year will enable us to extend the P.F.R.A. to British Columbia.

As a Liberal, I am not accustomed to those tactics. If that obstruction had come from fascists or communists, I would have said to myself, "Well, this is the natural course. They follow their principles. They are against freedom of speech." But the cornerstone of Liberalism is freedom of speech, and the speech of any member cannot be offensive to anyone who cannot understand the language in which it' is uttered. Therefore I could not understand why there was such objection to the speech by the hon. gentleman. I protest against those tactics. As a Liberal, I cannot conceive how anyone who
The Address-Mr. Pouliot

calls himself a Liberal should try to howl down anyone who thinks differently. I do not say that because the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche is one of the two members who compose his group. I have no particular interest in them. But he is a well-read member and a man of culture. He does not speak often in the house and it seems to me that, instead of anyone discouraging him from speaking, he should be encouraged to do so oftener, even by those who do not share his views.
With regard to freedom of speech, my main contention is that any hon. member should be given an opportunity to say all he has to say, within the rules, provided that those who answer him are given the same opportunity. There are 245 of us in the house, and naturally we cannot expect that all members should think alike. That is a complete impossibility. Besides that, I do not know that what happened last night would have been tolerated anywhere else, and Mr. Speaker did very well in stopping that performance.
But there is a thing we call retributive justice. There is the retaliation that fate brings to those who employ those tactics outside the house. Although I myself have never retaliated, I well remember the tactics of the Bloc Populaire in. the province of Quebec. They tried to break up meetings, a procedure to which I have been a witness on many occasions. I well recall an incident that occurred at Shawinigan Falls, the place where the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche lived. I went there with two of my colleagues, the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget) and the hon. member for Quebec West and South (Mr. Parent). We went there to hold a meeting. Naturally some of the key men of the Bloc Populaire were there, and they tried to break up our meeting. It took me half an hour of physical exertion to change the trend of the meeting. In the first place, they were jeering at the Liberal candidate, and there was such a tumult at a certain moment that I had to cover the microphone with my hand to speak to the crowd that was outside the hall. Those who were within the hall went outside to hear me speak through the loudspeaker. In the end, those outside were convinced that the speech was orthodox, and they got into the hall. And those very people who jeered at the Liberal candidate came to the stand to shake hands with him and congratulate him. They gave him an ovation. My friends, the hon. member for Levis and the hon. member for Quebec West and South, were witnesses of that incident which happened in the constituency of the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche.

I remember other instances in which the Bloc Populaire did not want those who did not share their views to express themselves. Those are not Liberal tactics. If the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche had some difficulty yesterday, it was precisely on account of retributive justice. He reminded me of Louis XVI who had to pay for the guilt of Louis XV. That is an old story. But I repeat that whoever tries to prevent a member from saying in this house what he has to say on behalf of his electors is not a Liberal and cannot claim to be a Liberal. I know that, with due afterthought, those who were guilty of that breach of the rules of the house will realize the significance of what they did last night, and will regret it. I do not say that in my own behalf, because I can handle my case alone. But I want to see a certain amount of dignity in this house, and I want the true principles of democracy maintained. How can anyone dare to speak of democracy when he prevents the other fellow from saying what he has to say? That sort of thing cannot go on in this house. Mr. Speaker stopped it, and I admired the way he performed his duty.
Well, that is for the Bloc Populaire, but there is something else about which we must be very careful, and that is the undermining of our democratic institutions by those who are not numerous enough to break up our meetings, and who seldom bring in outsiders to do so, but who every week or every other week write articles that tend to destroy the pillars of democracy in this country. They represent parliament as a wrong institution, as an institution full of dirt, as a place where no one is doing anything useful. Very often I disagree with my colleagues. Why should I be a yes man? Why should I be a rubber stamp in this house? I have my own views to express, but I believe everyone else has the right to express his views and try to convince the majority.

All the discussion that has occurred during the debate on the address has been interesting. Every speech has been a good one. However, some of the discussion has been entirely irrelevant. To be precise, I mean what has been said about Hong Kong. Before I close, I want to refer to my notes in order to tell the house what was said about this matter a long time ago. On January 22, 1942, I corrected the official report as follows:
Mr. Jean-Francois Pouliot (Temiscouata): Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, and
referring to page 4837 of Hansard of last session, the Hansard of yesterday, I am quoted there as follows:
"Mr. Pouliot:	The minister should resign
because of that fact." What I said was:
"The Minister of National Defence should resign om account of the Hong Kong affair."
The record is not complete because immediately after I had said that, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) shouted "Order" to prevent my saying anything further. That was, as always, a complete contradiction; he does not know what he wants.
I have before me a copy of the Conservative Toronto Telegram of January 23, 1942, the following day. I should like to quote from an editorial entitled, "Opposition forces the door to open inquiry into incompetence." The editorial reads:
It is not often that it is possible to agree with
J.	F. Pouliot, M.P., the effervescent member for Temiscouata, yet in his statement that the Minister of Defence should resign over the Hong Kong affair-a statement that was drowned by cries of "Order"-he appears to have been the only member of parliament who recognized the gravity of the situation revealed by the admissions of Honourable J. L. Ralston.
Then an advertisement appeared in the press asking young men to enlist in the Royal Rifles of Canada. This advertisement was silly because it was entitled, "Remember Hong Kong." The following appeared in the News of June 27, 1942, having been written by Judith Robinson:
. On February 5, Jean Francois Pouliot objected to a new recruiting poster which, beginning with the words: "Remember Hong Kong," announced that the Royal Rifles of Canada would be reconstituted 100 per cent. Mr. Pouliot considered it would be better that Canadian soldiers and sailors should forget Hong Kong, though the rest of us might remember it all our lives.
The advertisement was then changed to read:
Vengeons les heros de Hong Kong
We had three joint ministers of national defence who were equally responsible for the sending of unarmed troops to Hong Kong. What happened when I asked for the resignation of Colonel Ralston? I was howled down by the then leader of the opposition, Mr. Hanson, and by the other Conservative members. What happened afterwards? The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) went to Grey North and he eulogized the minister of national defence who was responsible for the sending of troops to Hong Kong. He was different from his illustrious predecessor, the then member for York-Sunbury, Mr. Hanson. Mr. Hanson did not want me to ask for the resignation of Ralston, but the hon. gentleman went further; he eulogized Ralston. In Grey North he said that Ralston was a great
The Address-Mr. Pouliot

man. How could he be a great man when he was responsible for the sending of unarmed troops to Hong Kong?
I have come back to the fold. The reason is that the three defence ministers who acted during the war had left the cabinet. If they had stayed in the cabinet I would have stayed outside the fold of the Liberal party. The other day we heard the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) speak about Hong Kong. He said that he wanted the whole correspondence tabled. For purely personal reasons I did not mention him at the time I asked for the resignation of Colonel Ralston. However, the Tory party applauded him. The Tory party applauded the hon. member who was one of the joint ministers of national defence. That being so, how can they come now and speak about the dismal Hong Kong affair?
The leader of the opposition and the members of the Conservative opposition are far from being logical. It is time to bring them down to fundamentals and tell them that one of the great rules of law is that no one can invoke his own turpitude. Many times during the war the Tory party and the few Conservative members who belonged to it were wrongly led by the then leader of the opposition. I will go further. When I spoke about the responsibility of a Tory senator who is now dead and who was inspector general of the western command; when I asked if he had done his duty, if it was his duty to see that these men were fully equipped, what did Ralston answer? He said it was none of his business. That was Ralston's business.
Now we hear a minister of the crown saying that Ralston is not here to defend himself. He was here when I denounced him and when he was unable to answer when I showed him the label from a bottle of John de Kuyper gin. How can a minister of the crown say that Ralston is out of the chamber now when he was here doing a wrong job and when I insisted upon his resignation? I did not get it, but finally, when, he and his two colleagues went out, I decided that it was time for me to come back to the fold. I will ask my hon. friends of the Conservative party as well as those of the Liberal party to realize that all the parties were guilty in the Hong Kong affair. I remember the time when the then leader of the opposition, Mr. Hanson, was saying from his seat as Conservative leader in this house: Why do we not send our men to all parts of the world so that they can share in every battle? That was said by the Conservative leader, who was the loud-speaker of Arthur Meighen, and who was never disowned or denied by anyone of the Conservative

party. I will tell the Conservative party to break their ties with the ugly past and think of the future, instead of indulging in such dismal practices.
The truth has come out, but we are not here to have a lecture on history. We have to think of the future, and when I think of the bright boys and girls of the coming generation I wonder if the thirty years I have spent in politics to advocate democracy, freedom and liberty have been wasted. They have been wasted for my generation, but I hope they have not been wasted for the generations to come.
I had the opportunity and the pleasure and the privilege of addressing groups of young Liberals in the province of Ontario and I realized that they are Liberals at heart. I realize that, in spite of the effort that has been made by long beards to enslave them into socialism, they are reluctant to get into it. They want to see the Liberal doctrine exemplified and put into practice in this country. Therefore, as a man who is getting old and has been a long time in politics, I give my confidence to the coming generation, which is much better than ours because they are more open-minded.
