subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDBESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I should like, first, to congratulate the mover (Mr. Dion) and the seconder (Mr. Dickey) of the address. Although we realize they did not have much material to work with we must commend them for the fine work they did.
In this debate the private member is allowed considerable latitude to discuss various subjects and tell something of the constituency which he has the honour to represent. I should like to say a few words about Durham county. We have heard many members say they represent the finest county in Canada, so that I think I should take this opportunity to tell the house about the best.
Durham county fronts on lake Ontario and is located about sixty miles east of Toronto and about 220 miles from this city. It was one of the first districts settled in the province, and I suggest that the settlers used good judgment. It was from Durham county in the early years that the finest lumber was shipped to England from our fine natural harbour at Port Hope. Even today there is a wooded area known as Mast Woods, from which was taken the tall, straight timbers which supplied masts for the British navy and their sailing ships.

The Address-Mr. Stephenson
Since the land was cleared, Durham county has become pre-eminently a diversified agricultural district, producing choice livestock, grain, tobacco and apples. Throughout the county there are many fine churches and schools; in the urban centres are located many fine factories which manufacture, for instance, rubber tires, conveyers, steel files, chemicals, fertilizers, leather goods, enamel ware, brass fittings, and a new factory has just been completed to manufacture compressors.
News is supplied to Durham county by several weekly newspapers and also dailies. I may say, in passing, that we have a daily paper in Port Hope which was first published in 1831, and has been published ever since, which I think is quite a record. We have also a weekly, the Canadian Statesman, the editorials of which are quoted all over Canada. It was awarded the EditoiV Trophy for the finest editorial last year on national unity. A signal honour was also conferred on the editor, Mr. George James, who won the silver medal given by the association of Canadian advertisers for the best contribution to advertising promotion in Canada in 1947. I think that is something we can all be proud of in Durham county.
I would be remiss if I did not mention that in Durham county is located the largest radium refinery in the world. Here also uranium is refined from which the atomic bomb is created. This new creation having served purposes of destruction, it is the hope of us all, even in the present state of the world that, through scientific research, this great energy-producing element may be used in the future for constructive instead of destructive purposes.
Durham county is a natural beauty spot. Its rolling hills are picturesque, while in the valleys flow spring-fed streams wherein sport the speckled trout. The inland lakes of Scugog and Rice provide the tourists with the big fellows such as muskellunge, pickerel and bass, which sometimes, of course, get away. On behalf of the citizens of Durham county I extend to all an invitation to visit this grand part of Canada.
I should like to make a few observations on our national problems. A, question that is asked of every member of the house and practically of all Canadians is this: How is it that we have side by side these two countries, Canada and the United States, separated by an imaginary boundary line; yet in the United States we find 145,000,000 people, while here in Canada we still have only 12,000,000? Is it because there has been no vision in this country? Is this why we are standing still with only 12,000,000 people? The fathers of confederation showed great vision for this
country. They realized that we must have railways and canals, and canals and railways were built to consolidate this great country east and west. Those railways were built under adverse circumstances, but the fathers of confederation had the vision and the courage to see that that task must be done. There has been some advancement made in this country, but we appear to have come to a period where all vision has been lost and not much encouragement is being given to explore our great natural resources. We know that we have the oil, the coal, and the minerals but very little encouragement is given to bringing these natural resources into production. That is why we have to buy these products today from the United States, which in turn is responsible for our adverse exchange position with that country. We have, over the past years, been selling our natural resources down the river for ten cents and buying them back in processed form for one dollar. That is one of the reasons why we have always had an adverse balance of trade with the United States.
Recently legislation was brought before the house to restrict some goods coming into Canada, thereby encouraging the production of materials in this country. I believe this is a step in the right direction, but it is a step which should have been taken many years ago. II we are to make a great nation of Canada we must have the vision and the courage to exploit our natural resources. The bill which was brought before the house was called, "An act to conserve foreign exchange." I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, the measure could better have been called, "An act to conserve and manufacture Canada's natural resources." I know the Liberal party would not accept that policy because it has been the policy of Conservative parties for years. The minister hesitated to say that the measure was a protectionist measure or a conservation measure, but he would rather give it the name of an emergency measure, which may come in today and go out tomorrow, leaving our manufacturers, and those who want to expand this country, in the position where they do not know when it is going out. What encouragement is that to our manufacturers and the people who try to produce things in this country?
I would say, sir, that twenty years ago, had the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King! not been so busy keeping his political ear to the ground and forming political strategy; had he been listening to the real needs of this country, we might not now find ourselves in the position in which we are today.
The Address-Mr. Stephenson

Over the doors of this parliament there is an inscription which no doubt all hon. members have seen. It reads, "Where there is no vision the people perish.'' I would suggest that these words might be well emblazoned across the walls of this chamber in order to remind the government and others in this country of the fact that where there is no vision the people perish. I maintain that what we need today in Canada is more vision.
The general opinion is abroad in this country that our frontiers have all been explored. I think that is an idea which should be removed because our children may possibly think that Canada has no further frontiers to explore, and therefore we find that they are drifting away from Canada and going to the United States. This is a question that we must all answer. Why is it that the United States has a population of 145,000,000 people today while we have barely 12,000,000? It is time that the government took off its political glasses in order that it might see the possibilities in Canada in their true light and do something about them.
I should also like to refer to the matter of immigration. The possible reason for our small population is that the government has had no immigration policy. It was interesting to note the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) when he spoke across the country lately. He told some of his audience that we should have and would have 500,000 people coming into this country every year, and this number would be eventually increased to one million people a year. The minister might have been talking politics, but it was interesting to note a recent item in the Globe and Mail, which showed that 48,000 immigrants were admitted to Canada last year. Something must be done f
to induce immigration into this country, because we know that today there are no tradesmen. If you want a tradesman today you cannot find him. There is no farm labour. It is impossible for the farmer to get help. I suggest to you, sir, that something must be done if we wish to increase industry in this country. According to a recent survey, the average age of the Ontario farmer is around sixty. I maintain that a man of this age cannot carry on and do all the work that is required of him to run a farm efficiently. That is the reason we are not getting the production in Ontario that we should have. The farmers have come to this position. During the war years they worked hard to produce everything for the war effort. They could not get the help they needed. Consequently they say, we will put in a little grain, feed a few hogs and cattle,, raise a few poultry and let it go at that. The result is that the land which should be worked today is going back to grass. Many of the farms are being abandoned. I would suggest that something be done immediately to procure farm labour for the farmers of Canada.
On motion of Mr. Stephenson the debate was adjourned.
Tomorrow we shall continue with this debate in the hope that it may be finished.
If it is concluded, what shall we take up later?
The Minister of Finance's emergency measure or the wheat bill.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
